observed_text:
Within Timken's roller-bearing discussion, the source distinguishes the two by examining the actual depression or wear area: false brinelling (fretting wear from slight axial rolling-element movement while stationary, or very small reversing angular oscillation) will wear away the surface texture, whereas the original surface texture remains in the depression of a true brinell, which the page-18 example caption describes as true metal deformation rather than wear [EV-K01-004]. The supplied CWT/category input (predicted_class 'outer_race') cannot establish which texture is physically present here: it is a caller-assigned class label, not a classifier or task-model inference, and the texture cue is a qualitative physical-surface inspection of the actual depression or wear area [EV-K01-004]. The scenario's assumed cause (external vibration during standstill) is an independently specified teaching assumption, not an observation, and temporal proximity does not establish causation [EV-K01-007]. General inspection guidance also directs examining raceways and external surfaces after thorough cleaning, but this is not a complete reuse or rejection rule [EV-K01-010].

Evidence limitations:
The texture comparison is a qualitative physical-surface inspection cue with no quantitative threshold; it cannot be applied from a class label alone [EV-K01-004].
The supplied CWT/category input is a caller-assigned label, not an actual classifier or task-model result, and no actual device records or inspectable sample pixels are supplied.
The assumed cause of external vibration during standstill is a teaching assumption, not an observation; temporal proximity does not establish causation [EV-K01-007].
Inspection guidance is generic bearing education only, not a complete reuse/replacement decision rule, and carries no model-specific thresholds or aviation/reuse authorization [EV-K01-010].
Source scope is generic bearing education with no transfer validation to CWRU artificial defects or aviation equipment.
